newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Pakistani rupee seen weak on speculative trade.
newsitem.headline: Pakistani rupee seen weak on speculative trade.

text.p: Pakistani rupee is likely to remain under pressure against the dollar amid speculative trade in the kerb market before the June 14 budget for fiscal 1997/98 (July-June), analysts said on Friday.

They said three lower adjustments by the State (central) Bank of Pakistan (SBP) since April 23 had prompted kerb players to speculate on the level the rupee would be before the close of the current fiscal year on June 30.
On Friday, the rupee opened 0.07 rupees up at 41.18 to the dollar in the kerb market amid profit-taking in the U.S. currency after posting sharp gains in the past few days.
The SBP rate, last changed on May 23, was 40.3900/40.5900 against the dollar. The rupee had lost 1.74 percent of its value in the kerb market since May 23.
"This is what happens when you do not adjust your currency value when it is needed," said a western economist, who asked not to be named.
"There is a substantial gap to bridge before the rupee achieves its real effective exchange rate and probably the market has sensed it," he said.
Bankers say the real effective exchange rate of the rupee had appreciated by 9.3 percent between last October and March while the nominal effective exchange rate soared 3.9 percent.
The SBP has depreciated the rupee by 0.67 percent since April 23, but kerb dealers say a further two to three percent devaluation is possible before the end of 1996/97.

"The rumours in the market are about a five percent one-step devaluation, but I think a three percent step-by-step devaluation before June 30 will be a more likely scenario," dealer Owais Kalia of Khanani & Kalia International said.

Kaleem Aziz, head of research at ING Baring Securities, said the rupee could be depreciated by about three percent if the SBP wanted to see it at a fair value and up to five percent if it wanted the rupee undervalued.
But he said the SBP might not go for a one-step devaluation and might cascade the required depreciation into the next four or five months when exports from Pakistan would remain slow.

"But if speculative buying of dollar in the kerb gains momentum and the gap between the market and official rate widens to above five percent, the schedule would not be sustainable and a faster depreciation would be needed," he said.
Dealer Ambreen Shaukat of KASB & Co said rumours of devaluation and sharp gains by dollar in the kerb had scared stock investors away from the market.
"Everyone is scared to put money at present because of the rupee devaluation," she said.
